title: From a .ps1 to a module
summary: Why teams ship functions as modules, what goes in a .psm1 and a .psd1 manifest, where PowerShell looks for modules, and how autoloading works.

steps.title: What a module gives you
body: Dot-sourcing a `.ps1` of helpers works for one person. A **module** is how a team shares functions:
- **one import, one version**: `Import-Module LogTools` (or just call a function: PowerShell loads the module
for you, *autoloading*);
- **public and private**: only the functions you export are visible; helpers stay internal;
- **a version and requirements** in a manifest, so `#Requires -Modules @{ ModuleName = 'LogTools'; ModuleVersion = '1.2' }`
and `Install-PSResource` mean something.
The parts:
| File | Holds |
| `LogTools.psm1` | the code: functions (the *root module*) |
| `LogTools.psd1` | the **manifest**: a hashtable with version, author, requirements and the export list |
| `Modules/LogTools/1.0.0/` | where it is installed: a folder per module, a subfolder per version |
PowerShell finds modules through **`$env:PSModulePath`**. For PowerShell 7 the per-user folder is
`Documents\PowerShell\Modules` on Windows and `~/.local/share/powershell/Modules` on Linux and macOS (Windows
PowerShell 5.1 uses `Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Modules`: another reason the two can see different modules).

steps.prompt: Why list functions explicitly in the manifest (`FunctionsToExport = 'Get-OldLog', 'Remove-OldLog'`) instead of `'*'`?
options: Autoloading can read the list without running the module, and private helpers stay private
PowerShell refuses to import modules that export `*`
Explicit lists make the functions run faster
steps.explain: With `'*'`, PowerShell must load and run the `.psm1` to discover what it exports, which slows down every `Get-Command` and Tab completion on a machine with many modules, and any helper function becomes public API that someone will start depending on.

steps.title: Writing the manifest
body: `New-ModuleManifest` writes a commented `.psd1` for you:
```powershell
$manifest = @{
Path              = './LogTools/LogTools.psd1'
RootModule        = 'LogTools.psm1'
ModuleVersion     = '1.0.0'
FunctionsToExport = 'Get-OldLog', 'Remove-OldLog'
Author            = 'Ops team'
Description       = 'Find and remove old log files.'
PowerShellVersion = '7.4'
New-ModuleManifest @manifest
Test-ModuleManifest ./LogTools/LogTools.psd1      # checks it, and shows what it exports
To try a module straight from your repo: `Import-Module ./LogTools/LogTools.psd1 -Force` (`-Force` reloads it after
you change the code; a plain `Import-Module` of an already loaded module does nothing). To *install* it for
yourself, copy the files to `<user module folder>/LogTools/1.0.0/`; from then on any session can just call
`Get-OldLog`. Later in this module you publish it to a feed instead, which is how teams really distribute it.

pairs: modules that must be loaded first
the oldest PowerShell it runs on

steps.title: Make LogTools a real module
prompt: `~/src/LogTools/LogTools.psm1` has three functions: `Get-OldLog`, `Remove-OldLog` and the private helper `Get-Cutoff`.
1. Create the manifest **`~/src/LogTools/LogTools.psd1`**: version **1.0.0**, root module `LogTools.psm1`, exporting
**only** `Get-OldLog` and `Remove-OldLog`, with an author, a description, and **PowerShell 7.4** as the minimum.

checks.name: the manifest is valid and says 1.0.0
it exports exactly the two public functions
checks.fail: The module should export `Get-OldLog` and `Remove-OldLog`, and keep `Get-Cutoff` private (`FunctionsToExport`).

checks.name: root module, description and minimum version
checks.fail: The manifest needs `RootModule = 'LogTools.psm1'`, `PowerShellVersion = '7.4'`, a `Description` and an `Author`.

checks.name: a new session finds it without Import-Module
checks.fail: From a fresh `pwsh`, `Get-OldLog -Path ~/logs/archive` should autoload the module from `~/.local/share/powershell/Modules/LogTools/1.0.0` and list the three old logs.

hints: Check it with `Test-ModuleManifest ~/src/LogTools/LogTools.psd1`, and `Import-Module ~/src/LogTools/LogTools.psd1 -Force; Get-Command -Module LogTools`.
solution: New-ModuleManifest -Path ~/src/LogTools/LogTools.psd1 -RootModule LogTools.psm1 -ModuleVersion 1.0.0 -FunctionsToExport Get-OldLog, Remove-OldLog -Author 'Ops team' -Description 'Find and remove old log files.' -PowerShellVersion 7.4
pwsh -NoProfile -c 'Get-OldLog -Path ~/logs/archive; Get-Module LogTools | Select-Object Name, Version, ModuleBase'
explain: `$env:PSModulePath -split [IO.Path]::PathSeparator` shows every folder PowerShell searches, in order. When two
versions are installed, `Import-Module` takes the highest unless you ask for one (`-RequiredVersion 1.0.0`), which
is how a team can roll a module forward and back.

steps.prompt: Reload your module from the repo after changing it, then list what it exports.
steps.explain: Without `-Force`, importing a module that is already loaded is a no-op, and you keep testing the old code: the classic "my fix did nothing" afternoon.

steps.prompt: A colleague installed your module into `Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Modules`. In `pwsh` it is "not found". Why?
options: That is Windows PowerShell 5.1's user module folder; PowerShell 7's is `Documents\PowerShell\Modules`
Modules must be installed for all users
PowerShell 7 cannot load modules written for 5.1
steps.explain: PowerShell 7 does include the Windows PowerShell module folders for *system* modules, but the per-user folders differ. Installing with `Install-PSResource -Scope CurrentUser` from `pwsh` puts it in the right place.
